description: Travertine is a Space Apps team from Denizli. For the Field Shift challenge we're building a tool that helps farmers decide what to plant and how to manage water using NASA data. I lead code and architecture (11 years in software, startup founder). Looking for: an agriculture or earth science student, a data analyst, a designer and a presenter. No experience required.
summary: Travertine is a live web tool that helps a farmer compare crop rotations for one field before committing a season. The farmer picks a field on a map and enters the rotation they grow now. Travertine runs 25 years of NASA POWER daily weather through an FAO-56 Penman-Monteith water balance for 12 crops and ranks alternative rotations on water, income, soil health and risk, always measured against the farmer's own rotation. Each suggestion states why it was suggested, the evidence behind it, its benefits, the information gaps and the risks that need local review. On our rain-fed demo field in Sarayköy, Denizli, continuous cotton leaves 69% of crop water demand unmet; a lentil, barley, lentil rotation leaves 4%. We tested the model against satellite vegetation records (MODIS NDVI) at six sites in four countries under a pre-registered protocol and publish the result with confidence intervals, including where it is not conclusive. Travertine works in English and Turkish, is open source under the MIT licence, and supports, but does not replace, farmer judgment and local expertise.
details:
LINKS

Live site: https://travertinefields.com

Source code (MIT licence): https://github.com/musbabaff/travertine

Public engine API: https://api.travertinefields.com/v1/health (OpenAPI contract in the repository)

THE PROBLEM

Farmers facing drier, hotter and less predictable seasons must decide what to plant years ahead. The climate and satellite records that could inform that decision exist, but they are scattered, coarse and written for specialists. A wrong rotation costs water, soil and a season's income.

WHAT TRAVERTINE DOES

1. The farmer picks a field on the map and says whether it is irrigated.

2. Travertine shows the field's climate, soil and vegetation record. Every number carries its dataset and its resolution, so coarse data is never presented as field-scale.

3. The farmer enters the rotation they grow now. It is scored with the same model as every alternative.

4. Travertine ranks 3 to 5 year rotations on four scores: water, income, soil health and risk. The farmer sets how much each one matters with sliders, and every alternative shows its difference from the current rotation.

5. Each rotation comes with five parts: why it was suggested, the evidence, the benefits, the information gaps, and the risks that need local review.

6. A sensitivity test replays the record with less rain or higher temperature (clearly labelled as not a forecast). The site also shows frost, heat and extreme-rain indices, a calendar of bare-field periods, and a printable rotation plan.

7. The farmer's own soil test can replace the global soil estimate.

8. Terms such as evapotranspiration, NDVI, frost risk and water balance are explained in plain language, on the page and by Cosmo, the site's guide.

EXAMPLE: DEMO FIELD, SARAYKÖY, DENİZLİ (11.6 ha, rain-fed)

Rainfall averages 631 mm a year against a reference evapotranspiration of 1,253 mm. Continuous cotton leaves 69% of crop water demand unmet (median of 22 three-year windows) and breaks three rotation rules; its overall score is 0.36. Lentil, barley, lentil leaves 4% unmet and scores 0.84.

HOW IT WORKS

- NASA POWER daily data (2001 to 2025) feeds the FAO-56 Penman-Monteith equation for reference evapotranspiration, then a daily root-zone water balance for each crop, using FAO-56 crop coefficients, stage lengths and root depths for 12 crops. Every coefficient is cited.

- Soil texture and organic carbon from ISRIC SoilGrids give the available water capacity (Saxton and Rawls 2006).

- Rotations are enumerated under agronomic rules and scored over every multi-year window of the record, so the farmer sees the median and the driest tenth of outcomes.

- Vegetation history comes from MODIS MOD13Q1 NDVI at 250 m and HLS (Landsat and Sentinel-2) NDVI at 30 m.

- Scores are relative rankings between 0 and 1. They are not yield or price forecasts.

HOW WE CHECKED IT

We asked whether years in which the model computes more unmet water demand are also years with lower satellite-observed greenness, and compared the model with a simple dryness index as a baseline. The protocol was written before the results were computed. Of eight registered sites, six could be computed (three in Türkiye, one each in Spain, France and Romania); two had no SoilGrids estimate.

- Pooled over six sites: model mean r = -0.60 (95% CI -0.70 to -0.50); baseline mean r = -0.49 (-0.61 to -0.37); difference -0.11 (-0.20 to -0.02).

- The pooled difference is established. Per site it is established only at Bărăgan, Romania. At the demo field the difference is -0.14 (-0.34 to +0.03), which is not established.

The site's Evidence page shows all of this, including the sites where the result is not conclusive.

LIMITS

NASA POWER describes the climate of a grid cell of about 0.5 degrees, not of one field. SoilGrids is a global estimate. The income score uses relative market values, not local prices. The validation uses greenness as a proxy; it is not a yield validation. Travertine supports, and does not replace, farmer judgment and local expertise.

BUILT WITH

Web: Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, MapLibre GL, visx, three.js. Engine: Python, FastAPI, NumPy, pandas, SciPy. Tests: 126 engine tests, web unit and end-to-end tests, accessibility checks. Hosting: Vercel, Render, Cloudflare. English and Turkish throughout.

USE OF AI

- Code and documentation: Claude Code (Anthropic) and OpenAI Codex coding agents wrote most of the code and documentation under our direction. Every change went through a pull request with automated tests and human review.

- Planning and writing: Claude (Anthropic) helped us plan the work and draft the slides and this text. The team checked every statement and number against the live engine.

- The results are not AI-generated. Every number on the site comes from deterministic, published methods (FAO-56) applied to NASA and partner data.

- Cosmo, the guide on the site, answers from fixed, checked text and from values computed by our engine. An optional mode that uses Google Gemini exists in the code but is switched off on the live site.

- No NASA logos or branding are used. Full statement: docs/AI_USE.md in the repository.

NEXT

Accounts and saved fields, regional crop and price data, terrain and erosion, a mobile app.

TEAM

Mustafa Babayev and Kemal Gencel (development), Azra Özkan (research support). Cosmo, the mascot of the Denizli event, appears on the site with the organisers' permission.
